zoom_grid.caption: **12 random rigs, 20 s each.** One airborne sample per posterior draw (`posterior.json` + `draws/*.json`), each panel on its own y-range because the drawn operating points span 96-213 rev/s. Rotor colours are the mixer order.

flight_grid.caption: **6 random rigs, whole flights.** `full_flight(179 s)` per draw — the length is the median over rigs of the rig's longest recording. A draw carries airborne parameters only, so every level the whole-flight wrapper needs is the mean fitted ratio over the fitted rigs times the draw's own `mu` (idle_rps = 0.31 x mu, rps_max = 1.42 x mu, rps_min = 0.60 x mu); every other phase is the shared `flight.wrap_airborne` scaffold.

planes.caption: **Where the draws sit relative to the rigs.** Three planes of the rig vector: the operating point against the relative airborne spread, the collective mode's oscillator (`f0`, `zeta`), and its slow component (`tau_slow`, `sigma_slow`). Red diamonds are the 7 fitted rigs, grey dots the 12 draws. The posterior is a diagonal Gaussian in scale-free coordinates with a floored per-coordinate width, so the draws must spread wider than the rigs — with 7 drones the raw spread would be far too tight to sample from.

zoom.caption: **All 7 rigs at a glance, 20 s each.** Each row is one rig. The left cell is its real telemetry, the middle cell is the current sampler fitted to that rig, the right cell is the new model fitted to that rig. A row shares one y-range across its three cells, so the cells are directly comparable. Rotor colours are the mixer order in every cell. Row scales differ, because the rigs run from 78 to 278 rev/s.

flight.caption: **All 7 rigs at a glance, whole flights.** Each row is one rig. The left cell is its real telemetry, the middle cell is the current sampler fitted to that rig, the right cell is the new model fitted to that rig. A row shares one y-range across its three cells, so the cells are directly comparable. Rotor colours are the mixer order in every cell. Row scales differ, because the rigs run from 78 to 278 rev/s. explore.caption: DREGON's `motor.measured` is a ~45 Hz sample-and-hold, not a 1002 Hz measurement: 95.3 % of consecutive native samples are bit-identical and the measured-minus-command residual accounts for 106 % of the 5-15 Hz band variance. Above ~5 Hz the channel shows its own staircase.

Michael's telemetry has the opposite defect: 1 RPM amplitude steps (0.02 % of the operating point) but only a 29.41 Hz log rate, partly held (P(delta = 0) ~ 0.42, median hold 68 ms). The 12-14.7 Hz band sits 2000x above the quantisation floor, so the near-Nyquist content is folding and hold-resampling, not shaft motion.
A DJI M100's rotor speed is a nearly featureless power law: the best hump in the band is +2.0 dB at 8.70 Hz with no -3 dB crossing inside the band, broadband slope -20.9 dB/decade.

The only clean resonance in the corpus is in the DREGON command channel: +4.3 dB at 3.00 Hz, -3 dB width 2.80-3.30 Hz (Q ~ 6), second peak 6.7 dB. That is the MikroKopter attitude loop. A resonance must therefore be a per-rig parameter that is allowed to vanish.

The four control modes do not share a spectral shape. The collective and yaw modes carry 78 % of the rotor variance, roll and pitch sit ~10 dB below across the whole band, and the leading eigenvector is a collective/yaw mixture (cosines 0.55 / 0.67), not a mixer column.
The autocorrelation has two time scales — 0.98 at 0.02 s, 0.82 at 0.1 s, 0.16 at 1 s, 0.007 at 10 s, 1/e crossing 0.43 s — so no single exponential (AR(1)) fits it.
